metadata.title: Reverse Kesa-Gatame Bottom | BJJ Position Guide | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Master Reverse Kesa-Gatame Bottom escape techniques. Complete defensive guide covering frames, hip escapes, and transitions with 45% beginner escape rate.

overview:
Reverse Kesa-Gatame Bottom is a defensive position where the practitioner is pinned underneath an opponent who has secured reverse scarf hold control. Unlike traditional Kesa Gatame where the top player's hips face toward the bottom player's head, in Reverse Kesa-Gatame the top player's hips face toward the legs, creating a different set of control mechanics and escape opportunities. This position is characterized by the top player sitting on the bottom player's chest/shoulder area while controlling the near arm and facing toward the bottom player's hips and legs.

The bottom player faces significant challenges in this position as their mobility is severely restricted, with one arm typically trapped and their upper body compressed. However, the position offers distinct escape pathways that differ from traditional scarf hold escapes, primarily exploiting the top player's weight distribution and the direction of their control. The key to survival and escape lies in maintaining defensive frames with the free arm, creating space through hip movement, and capitalizing on the top player's tendency to sit too high or commit too heavily to submissions.

From a strategic perspective, Reverse Kesa-Gatame Bottom requires immediate defensive action to prevent the position from consolidating into more dominant pins like North-South or Mount. The bottom player must prioritize hip escape mechanics, frame construction with the free arm, and systematic space creation before attempting to recover guard or transition to a neutral position. Understanding the biomechanics of this pin and the specific vulnerabilities it creates is essential for developing an effective escape system.
state_invariants: Bottom player is on their back or side with shoulders pinned or near the mat, facing significant upper body compression from top player's weight distributed through hips and torso positioned across chest and shoulder area

Top player sits perpendicular or reverse-perpendicular to bottom player's torso with hips facing toward bottom player's legs, maintaining chest-to-chest pressure while controlling near-side arm through various grips (wrist control, underhook, or arm wrap)

Bottom player's mobility is severely restricted in upper body with one arm typically trapped or controlled, while far-side arm and lower body retain some freedom of movement for defensive frames and hip escapes
Top player's weight creates downward pressure on bottom player's chest, diaphragm, and shoulder complex, making breathing difficult and limiting rotation toward the trapped side

Opponent has established reverse scarf hold grips and positioning
Bottom player's upper body is pinned with limited mobility
Near-side arm is controlled or trapped by opponent
key_principles: Immediately establish defensive frames with free arm to prevent opponent from fully settling weight and consolidating control
Protect neck and head from submission attempts (arm triangle, baseball choke, neck cranks) by keeping chin tucked and maintaining space between shoulder and neck
Create space through systematic hip escape movements, shrimping away from opponent's weight to gradually extract trapped shoulder and arm
Use bridge and turn mechanics to disrupt opponent's base and weight distribution, particularly targeting vulnerabilities when they sit too high or lean too far forward
Prevent opponent from transitioning to more dominant positions (North-South, Mount, or full side control) by controlling distance with frames and blocking hip movement
Maintain awareness of submission threats specific to reverse scarf hold while executing escape sequences, never abandoning defensive posture for aggressive escaping
Systematically work to recover guard position rather than attempting to immediately stand or scramble, prioritizing positional safety over explosive escapes

common_errors.error: Flat on back with no frames established
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to fully settle weight and consolidate control, making escapes exponentially more difficult and exposing neck to chokes
common_errors.correction: Immediately establish frame with free arm against opponent's hip or shoulder, turn slightly onto side away from opponent to create angle for hip escape

common_errors.error: Attempting explosive bridge without proper setup
common_errors.consequence: Wastes energy and often results in opponent transitioning to more dominant position like Mount or North-South when bridge fails
common_errors.correction: Only bridge when opponent's weight is committed too far forward; combine bridge with grip fighting to off-balance before explosive movement

common_errors.error: Ignoring submission defense while focusing on escape
common_errors.consequence: Gets caught in arm triangle, Americana, or Kimura while attempting to escape, losing position and match
common_errors.correction: Maintain chin tucked, protect trapped arm, and keep free arm ready to defend neck; escape systematically rather than desperately

common_errors.error: Pulling trapped arm without creating space first
common_errors.consequence: Arm remains stuck and pulling motion often makes opponent's control tighter, potentially damaging shoulder joint
common_errors.correction: Create space through hip escape and frame before attempting to extract arm; use shrimping motion to gradually free shoulder

common_errors.error: Bringing far knee toward opponent in escape attempt
common_errors.consequence: Feeds leg to opponent for transition to Mount or knee-on-belly, worsening position significantly
common_errors.correction: Keep far leg posted on mat for base; use near-side leg to shrimp and create distance while far leg maintains stable platform

common_errors.error: Neglecting to control opponent's far arm
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent to post freely for base or establish grips for submissions and position advancement
common_errors.correction: Use free arm to control opponent's far arm or wrist when possible, limiting their options and making escapes more effective

training_drills.name: Progressive Resistance Escape Drill
training_drills.description: Partner applies Reverse Kesa-Gatame with increasing levels of resistance (30%, 50%, 70%, 100%) while bottom player works through systematic escape sequence: frame establishment, hip escape, arm extraction, guard recovery. Each resistance level practiced for 2-minute rounds.

training_drills.description: Partner holds Reverse Kesa-Gatame and actively attacks with Americana, Kimura, and Arm Triangle while bottom player maintains defensive posture and works escapes. training_drills.description: Bottom player must escape Reverse Kesa-Gatame within 60 seconds (beginners), 45 seconds (intermediates), or 30 seconds (advanced) while partner provides realistic resistance. Tracks success rate and identifies most reliable escape paths under time pressure.

training_drills.name: Bridge and Roll Timing Drill
training_drills.description: Partner sits in varying heights and weight distributions in Reverse Kesa-Gatame while bottom player practices recognizing optimal bridge timing. Focus on explosive hip extension only when opponent's weight is committed too far forward. 10 repetitions per round.

expert_insights.danaher: Reverse Kesa-Gatame Bottom represents a high-pressure defensive scenario where systematic escape methodology must override panic responses. The biomechanical reality is that the top player's weight distribution creates a specific vector of pressure that can be exploited through precise hip escape mechanics combined with frame construction. The critical error most practitioners make is attempting to pull the trapped arm before creating the necessary space through shrimping movements. The proper sequence involves establishing a pushing frame with the free arm against the opponent's hip or shoulder, executing a shrimp to create initial space, and only then working to extract the trapped shoulder. The position's vulnerability lies in the top player's tendency to sit too high on the chest, which compromises their base and creates bridge opportunities. However, bridging should be viewed as a secondary option only when the opponent makes this specific error. The primary pathway should always be systematic hip escape to guard recovery, as this represents the highest percentage escape under most circumstances.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: From a competition standpoint, Reverse Kesa-Gatame Bottom is a position you absolutely cannot afford to stay in for extended periods. The submission threats are real and the position can score heavily for your opponent if they transition to Mount or Back. My approach is immediate and aggressive framing with the free arm while working a hip escape to at least get to half guard. The key is not to wait for the perfect moment - you need to create movement immediately because the longer you stay static, the more settled their weight becomes and the harder everything gets. I've found that most guys will try to transition to Mount or North-South from here rather than hunt for the submission, so you have to be ready to follow their movement and use their transition as your escape opportunity. When they start moving to improve position, that's when you shrimp hard and recover some kind of guard. The bottom line is this position is dangerous and you need to treat it with urgency - work your frames, work your hips, and get the hell out of there as fast as possible while staying technical.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Reverse Kesa-Gatame Bottom is one of those old school pins that people underestimate until they're stuck under a heavy pressure player who knows how to ride it. The traditional escape methods work, but I've found that incorporating some unconventional movements can really throw people off. One thing I teach is using the lockdown concept even from here - if you can get your far leg hooked over their near leg while you're working the escape, it kills their ability to transition to Mount and gives you some control over their lower body. Another option that works in no-gi is to actually go inverted temporarily - if they're sitting too high and you can't get the standard shrimp going, sometimes going to a pseudo-granby position and threatening to come up on top or take their back can force them to abandon the position. The key is staying creative and not getting married to one escape sequence. If the first path isn't working, have three or four backup plans ready to go. This position is about survival first, then escape, then maybe getting wild with some inversions if you've got the flexibility and timing.

overview:
Reverse Kesa Gatame is a controlling pin position where you are positioned perpendicular to your opponent but facing away from their head, with your hip applying pressure to their chest or shoulder area. This position is the reverse configuration of traditional Kesa Gatame (scarf hold), offering unique control and submission opportunities with different mechanical advantages. Unlike standard Kesa Gatame where you face toward the opponent's head, Reverse Kesa Gatame positions you facing their legs, creating isolation of the far arm and unique attacking angles for arm locks, particularly the Americana and Kimura.

This position excels at controlling opponents who attempt to turn into you during side control exchanges, and provides excellent transitional control when moving between North-South and traditional side control positions. The reverse orientation creates strong pressure through the hips into the opponent's chest while simultaneously controlling their near arm and isolating their far arm for attacks. The position's effectiveness lies in its ability to distribute weight through the hips directly onto the opponent's sternum and shoulder, making breathing difficult and escapes challenging.

Reverse Kesa Gatame is particularly valuable in no-gi grappling where traditional collar-based controls are unavailable, and serves as a high-percentage attacking position for intermediate to advanced practitioners who understand proper weight distribution and arm isolation mechanics.

common_errors.error: Placing weight through hands instead of hips, reducing pressure on opponent's chest
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can breathe easily and create frames with arms to push your hips away and escape
common_errors.correction: Keep hands light and mobile, driving all weight through hips directly into opponent's sternum and shoulder complex

common_errors.error: Positioning hips too high on opponent's chest near their neck area
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can bridge explosively using their hips to create angles and roll you over
common_errors.correction: Keep hips centered on opponent's mid-chest to sternum area where bridges are less effective and pressure is maximized

common_errors.error: Failing to control opponent's near arm, leaving it free to create frames
common_errors.consequence: Opponent uses near arm to push against your hip or body, creating space for shrimping escapes
common_errors.correction: Secure near arm under your armpit or control with firm grip, isolating it from defensive use

common_errors.error: Keeping legs too close together reducing base width and stability
common_errors.consequence: Opponent can bridge effectively and generate enough force to roll you over or create angles
common_errors.correction: Sprawl legs wide with one extended fully for anti-bridge stability and one providing rotational control

common_errors.error: Raising head and chest up away from opponent creating space underneath
common_errors.consequence: Opponent creates frames and escapes by shrimping into the space between your chest and their body
common_errors.correction: Keep chest and head low, tight to opponent's body, chest facing toward their legs with minimal space

common_errors.error: Focusing solely on submission attacks while neglecting positional control and pressure
common_errors.consequence: Opponent escapes during submission attempts because base and pressure were compromised prematurely
common_errors.correction: Establish dominant control first with heavy hip pressure and arm isolation before attempting submissions

common_errors.error: Allowing opponent to turn toward you during transition from side control
common_errors.consequence: Opponent recovers guard by getting their knees between you and completing the escape sequence
common_errors.correction: Drive hips forward as opponent turns, transitioning to North-South or mount before guard recovery completes

training_drills.name: Static Pressure Maintenance Drill
training_drills.description: Partner lies flat on back while you establish Reverse Kesa Gatame position. Hold position for 2-minute rounds focusing solely on maintaining heavy hip pressure, proper weight distribution, and near arm control. Partner remains passive initially, then adds light resistance (breathing, small movements). Goal is to maintain position without using excessive energy while preventing any space creation.

training_drills.name: Dynamic Escape Defense Drill
training_drills.description: Start in established Reverse Kesa Gatame position with partner attempting specific escape sequences (bridge and roll, elbow escape, shrimp to guard). You must maintain position and counter each escape attempt by adjusting base, redistributing pressure, or transitioning to mount/North-South. Partner uses progressive resistance from 50% to 100% over multiple rounds. Focus on timing your adjustments to opponent's movements.

training_drills.name: Submission Chain Drill
training_drills.description: From Reverse Kesa Gatame, flow through submission sequence: Americana attempt → Kimura when opponent defends → North-South Choke if opponent turns → Mount transition if opponent creates space. Partner provides realistic defensive reactions to each attack. Practice smooth transitions between submissions without losing control. Emphasizes maintaining pressure while attacking.

training_drills.name: Position Entry Drill
training_drills.description: Start from various positions (side control, North-South, knee on belly, scrambles) and practice entering Reverse Kesa Gatame. Partner provides moderate resistance. Focus on timing the entry when opponent turns into you, proper hip placement for immediate pressure, and securing near arm control during transition. Develop ability to recognize and capitalize on opportunities to enter this position.

expert_insights.danaher: Reverse Kesa Gatame represents an excellent example of how reversing traditional positioning creates entirely new mechanical advantages and submission opportunities. The critical insight here is that by facing toward the opponent's legs rather than their head, you fundamentally change the geometry of arm isolation and control. The far arm becomes naturally isolated due to your body position, making it exceptionally vulnerable to Americana and Kimura attacks without requiring complex setups. The biomechanics of this position favor the top player significantly - your hip pressure works directly against the opponent's breathing muscles and ribcage, while their ability to generate escape force is severely compromised by the perpendicular angle and arm control. What makes this position particularly valuable is its transitional nature - it serves as an excellent midpoint between side control and North-South, allowing you to flow between positions based on opponent reactions while maintaining dominant control throughout. The key technical element is understanding that hip pressure, not chest pressure, creates the control here. Many practitioners make the error of trying to use upper body weight when the power of this position comes from driving the hips downward into the opponent's sternum and shoulder complex.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: In competition, Reverse Kesa Gatame is one of my favorite positions when opponents try to turn into me from side control because it gives me immediate attacking opportunities without complicated setups. The position is especially effective in no-gi where you can't rely on collar grips, and the direct hip pressure creates incredible control. I use this position primarily as a submission hunting ground - the Americana is right there if they leave the far arm extended, and if they defend by pulling the arm tight, I immediately switch to Kimura control or transition to mount. The key competitive insight is that this position tires opponents out extremely quickly because of the pressure on their breathing, so even if I don't get the immediate submission, I'm setting up my attacks for later in the match when they're exhausted. In my matches, I've found that holding this position for 30-45 seconds makes opponents desperate to escape, which opens up either the submission or an easy transition to mount or back control. The mistake I see competitors make is trying to force submissions too quickly - establish the control first, let the pressure do its work, then attack when they make mistakes trying to breathe or escape.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Reverse Kesa Gatame fits perfectly into the 10th Planet philosophy of using unconventional positions and angles to create submissions that opponents don't expect or train for regularly. What I love about this position is that most people spend all their time drilling escapes from standard side control and Kesa Gatame, but when you reverse the orientation, their muscle memory doesn't work the same way and they make mistakes. The position creates natural opportunities for shoulder locks and arm attacks, but where it gets really interesting is using it as a transition point to more advanced positions like the Truck or Twister control when they try to turtle out. In no-gi especially, this position is money because you're not dependent on gi grips and the slippery nature of skin-on-skin contact actually works in your favor with the hip pressure. I teach my students to think of Reverse Kesa as a hunting position - you're waiting for the opponent to move wrong, and when they do, you've got multiple attacks ready. The innovative approach is combining this with lockdown-style leg control if you catch them in transition - you can create a modified Reverse Kesa with lockdown that's extremely difficult to escape and sets up unique submissions that most competitors have never seen.

overview: Reverse Kesa Gatame (Reverse Scarf Hold) is a dominant pinning position where the top practitioner faces away from the opponent's head while maintaining chest-to-chest pressure and controlling the opponent's far arm. This position is particularly effective for shutting down common side control escapes while providing unique submission opportunities and transitions. The reverse orientation creates different mechanical advantages compared to traditional scarf hold positions, specifically eliminating the opponent's ability to frame against your face and neck. From this position, the top player can apply crushing chest pressure, isolate the far arm for submissions, and transition to mount, north-south, or back control. The position is especially valuable against defensive opponents who excel at creating frames from bottom side control.
state_invariants: Top player's chest maintains heavy contact with opponent's upper torso, creating constant downward pressure through the sternum and pectoral muscles onto opponent's ribcage and shoulder complex
Top player's back and shoulders face toward opponent's head while hips remain low and heavy on opponent's near-side ribs, creating a reverse orientation that eliminates traditional framing options
Opponent's far arm is trapped either under top player's armpit with elbow clamped tight to ribs, or controlled with deep overhook grip that prevents arm extraction and defensive hand fighting
Top player's legs are configured in wide base with far leg extended and near leg bent, providing stable platform against bridge attempts while maintaining hip pressure on opponent's torso
Opponent remains flat on back with shoulders pinned to mat, unable to turn into top player or establish guard due to combination of chest pressure and arm isolation
prerequisites: Successful guard pass or transition from standard side control position
Control of opponent's far arm established before rotating into reverse position
Understanding of weight distribution and pressure application through chest and hips
Ability to maintain balance and base while facing away from opponent's head
Recognition of optimal timing to enter reverse kesa from side control transitions
key_principles: Reverse Orientation Control: Facing away from opponent's head eliminates their ability to use frames against your face and neck while creating unique submission angles
Arm Isolation Dominance: Trapping the far arm under your armpit or with overhook removes opponent's primary defensive tool and opens submission pathways
Hip Pressure Application: Low hip position pressed against opponent's ribs prevents shrimp escapes and guard recovery while creating breathing difficulty
Chest Compression Control: Direct chest-to-chest pressure through sternum restricts breathing and creates maximum discomfort with sustainable effort
Base Management Through Legs: Wide leg configuration with strategic positioning provides stability against bridge and roll attempts while maintaining mobility for transitions
Weight Distribution Strategy: Concentrating pressure points on opponent's torso and shoulder creates maximum control efficiency without exhausting top player
Escape Prevention Through Position: Reverse position naturally blocks common side control escape pathways including elbow escape, ghost escape, and guard recovery

Else if opponent attempts to bridge and create space upward

common_errors.error: Sitting too upright with elevated chest and hips raised off opponent
common_errors.consequence: Reduces chest pressure on opponent, allowing them to breathe more easily and create space. Upright posture also makes you vulnerable to being rolled or swept, as your center of gravity is too high. Opponent can more easily turn into you and recover guard.
common_errors.correction: Keep your chest low and heavy on opponent's torso, maintaining constant downward pressure. Your shoulders should be lower than your hips, creating a forward lean that maximizes weight distribution. Think about melting your chest into their upper body. If opponent can breathe normally or is attempting to bridge, you're likely too upright.

common_errors.error: Losing control of the trapped far arm
common_errors.consequence: Opponent immediately uses freed arm to create frames, push your face, or establish defensive grips. This drastically reduces your control effectiveness and opens multiple escape pathways. The trapped arm is your primary control mechanism - losing it means losing the position advantage.
common_errors.correction: Maintain constant tension on the trapped arm, either by clamping it under your armpit with elbow tight to your body, or with a firm overhook grip. Your armpit clamp should be complete - the arm must be fully secured, not just touching. You should feel resistance if opponent tries to extract their arm.

common_errors.error: Narrow base with legs too close together
common_errors.consequence: Unstable platform makes you vulnerable to bridge and roll escapes. Opponent can generate enough force to tip you over or create space for guard recovery. Narrow base also limits your ability to distribute weight effectively.
common_errors.correction: Extend your far leg wide and long for maximum base width. Near leg should be bent but positioned to provide lateral stability. Your legs should form a wide tripod with your hips, creating a stable platform that's difficult to upset. Adjust base width based on opponent's escape attempts.

common_errors.error: Facing too far toward opponent's legs rather than perpendicular
common_errors.consequence: Reduces chest-to-chest pressure and makes it easier for opponent to turn into you. Poor angle also limits your submission options and makes transitions less effective. You lose the primary advantage of the reverse position.
common_errors.correction: Your back should face directly toward opponent's head with your chest perpendicular to their centerline. Your sternum should press into their upper chest/shoulder area. Maintain this perpendicular angle while keeping hips low and base wide.

common_errors.error: Using arms to post and support weight instead of chest pressure
common_errors.consequence: Reduces the crushing chest pressure that makes this position so effective. Arm posting also tires your upper body quickly and signals to opponent that you're not applying maximum pressure. Your arms should be free for transitions and submissions, not supporting your weight.
common_errors.correction: Let your chest and core do the work of maintaining pressure. Your weight should rest through your torso onto opponent's chest. Arms should be light, ready to control opponent's movements or attack submissions. If your arms are tired, you're using them too much for posting.

common_errors.error: Staying static in position without threatening submissions or transitions
common_errors.consequence: Allows opponent time to develop escape strategy and wait for opportunities. Referees may stand you up for stalling. Static control without advancement doesn't capitalize on the position's offensive potential.
common_errors.correction: Constantly threaten submissions (kimura, americana, arm triangle) or position advancements (mount, north-south, back). Even if you're not finishing, the threat of attack prevents opponent from relaxing and planning escapes. Move through submission threats in cycles to maintain offensive pressure.

training_drills.name: Transition Sequence Practice

expert_insights.danaher: Reverse kesa gatame represents a sophisticated understanding of pin mechanics where orientation reversal fundamentally alters the defensive options available to bottom player. The critical mechanical advantage lies in eliminating the opponent's ability to create frames against your head and neck - their primary defensive tools from traditional side control positions. When executing this position, focus on three biomechanical priorities: first, chest-to-chest compression through your sternum directly onto their ribcage creates breathing difficulty that accumulates over time; second, isolation of the far arm removes their strongest defensive tool and opens kimura, americana, and arm triangle pathways; third, hip pressure positioned low on their ribs prevents the shrimp escape that is the foundation of most guard recovery sequences. The position is particularly effective against modern guard players who have developed excellent framing systems from bottom side control. Your weight distribution should be approximately 70% through your chest onto their torso, with the remaining 30% distributed through your hips and base. This creates maximum control while maintaining the mobility necessary for transitions to mount, north-south, or back control when opponent attempts escape.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: I use reverse kesa gatame specifically against opponents who have good defensive frames from bottom side control. When their frames are getting in my face, I'll switch to reverse kesa to neutralize that defense entirely. The position is excellent for wearing down opponents - the chest pressure is brutal and sustainable for the top person. I typically hold this position to accumulate control time or fatigue my opponent, then transition to mount or back when I feel them weakening. The kimura from here is particularly high percentage because they can't defend with their trapped arm. In competition, I'll often use this as a recovery position if I'm losing grips or feeling my side control getting compromised - rotating to reverse kesa resets the escape attempts and gives me fresh control options. The key is not staying here too long - use it to break their defense, threaten submissions to create reactions, then advance to mount or take the back when they give you the opportunity. Against high-level opponents, I'm usually only holding reverse kesa for 15-30 seconds before transitioning, but that's enough time to drain their energy and set up the next attack.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: Reverse kesa is sick for setting up submissions, especially if you're hunting that shoulder compression and arm attacks. What I like about this position is that it confuses people - they're not used to defending against someone with their back turned, so their standard escape sequences don't work the same way. You can flow into some nasty arm locks and shoulder cranks that they don't see coming because the angles are different than what they've drilled a thousand times. I'll often use this as a transitional position when hunting for the truck or twister positions - if they start defending the twister side control, reverse kesa is right there as a backup control position. The key is keeping your weight heavy and your base wide - don't let them buck you off. From here you can threaten the kimura, which makes them defend, and when they defend the kimura you can transition to mount or spin to north-south for the choke. It's all about creating dilemmas - they can't defend everything at once. In no-gi especially, this position is money because without the gi grips they can't establish the same defensive frames they use from regular side control. Keep the pressure constant, stay heavy on that chest, and when they try to escape, that's when you capitalize with the transition or submission.
